title: Building Multi-Task Agentic LLMs via Two-Phase Distillation

paper.title: Building Multi-Task Agentic LLMs via Two-Phase Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract A key step toward artificial general intelligence is to train models that can perform multiple tasks. In this paper, we study how to build such models by first training separate RL experts for individual tasks and then consolidating them via distillation, as an alternative to directly training a single model on mixed tasks. We show that off-policy distillation degrades in multi-task settings due to the mode-covering nature of forward KL: aggregating data from multiple tasks introduces a large number of behavioral modes that can exceed the student’s capacity, forcing it to average across behaviors and leading to degraded performance. In contrast, on-policy distillation is mode-seeking but requires strong initialization.
Inspired by these observations, we propose a two-phase approach: off-policy distillation followed by on-policy refinement.
Evaluation across conversational agents and text-based games confirms that this two-phase approach matches single-task RL expert performance for each individual task, whereas off-policy or on-policy distillation alone fails to match this performance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success across a wide range of agentic large language model (LLM) tasks, including interactive tool-using agents ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , search agents ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , and text-based games ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . As an important step towards artificial general intelligence, LLMs are expected to solve multiple tasks simultaneously. However, building such unified multi-task models remains challenging. A straightforward approach is multi-task RL, i.e., jointly training a single model on multiple tasks. Unfortunately, multi-task RL presents significant practical challenges. Wu et al. (2025) find that different tasks may exhibit vastly different gradient scales, yet larger gradients do not necessarily correlate with greater performance gains. Ramesh et al. (2026) observe that certain tasks can dominate the training process, leading to suboptimal multi-task performance. Furthermore, multi-task RL may incur substantial computational costs, as the training cost of each trial is comparable to the sum of training all individual tasks. An alternative solution is to train one expert model for each task and then combine these models into a unified model. Two primary approaches exist for such combination: parameter merging ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) and distillation ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . While parameter merging offers computational efficiency by requiring little or no additional training, it operates as a black box with limited interpretability. Parameter merging often suffers from performance trade-offs between tasks ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Empirically, we observe substantial performance degradation with parameter merging on the benchmarks we evaluate. Additionally, the effectiveness of parameter merging is highly sensitive to the training dynamics of the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase. (See Appendix B.1 for details.) This paper focuses on distillation-based methods, which provide a more interpretable paradigm for combining knowledge from different expert models. We consider two main distillation approaches: off-policy and on-policy distillation. Off-policy distillation collects rollouts from teacher models and applies supervised fine-tuning, essentially optimizing the forward KL divergence. In contrast, on-policy distillation samples from the student model and optimizes the reverse KL divergence.

sections.heading: Limitations of Off-Policy and On-Policy Distillation.
sections.text: Comparing off-policy and on-policy distillation, off-policy distillation is easier to implement and offers better training stability, but prior work has identified several limitations of off-policy distillation: (1) exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , where the student model makes out-of-distribution errors during generation but receives no guidance on recovery from the training data, causing errors to accumulate across generation steps; (2) mode-covering behavior ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , which typically occurs when the teacher has larger capacity than the student—since off-policy distillation optimizes forward KL (a mode-covering objective), the student model is incentivized to place probability mass across all modes in the teacher distribution, including placing excessive probability on low-probability regions; (3) conflicting reasoning structures between teacher and student ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Among these possible limitations of off-policy distillation, our experiments reveal that when building multi-task agentic LLMs, the major challenge likely stems from its mode-covering property. Even when the student and teacher models share the same base model, aggregating data from multiple tasks introduces a larger number of behavioral modes that can exceed the student model’s capacity, forcing it to compromise by averaging across modes. Conversely, on-policy distillation cannot be applied directly without proper initialization, as it requires the student model to already possess sufficiently strong performance to generate reasonable trajectories.

sections.heading: Our Method: Two-Phase Distillation.
sections.text: To address this limitation, we propose a two-phase distillation approach: off-policy distillation followed by on-policy refinement. The mode-seeking property of on-policy distillation enables the student model to focus on a subset of modes, mitigating the averaging behavior induced by off-policy distillation. Meanwhile, off-policy distillation provides the necessary initialization for on-policy distillation to generate reasonable trajectories. We evaluate our method on four tasks: two conversational agent domains from τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench ( Barres et al., 2025 ) and two text-based games from GEM ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , demonstrating that our approach successfully recovers the performance of single-task RL models. Additionally, we investigate data aggregation strategies for multi-task off-policy distillation, showing that while data mixture affects off-policy distillation performance, our two-phase approach remains robust across different mixture configurations.

sections.heading: 2.1 Knowledge Distillation
sections.text: Distillation transfers knowledge from a teacher model to a student model through two primary approaches. Off-policy distillation, also known as supervised knowledge distillation, collects data from the teacher model and applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . Recent successes ( Guha et al., 2025 ; Moshkov et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2025 ) have demonstrated that off-policy distillation enables small models (e.g., 1.5B parameters) to acquire strong reasoning capabilities for complex tasks in mathematics, coding, and science. However, as argued by Agarwal et al. (2024) , the mode-covering nature of forward KL divergence in off-policy distillation can cause the student to assign excessive probability mass to low-probability regions of the teacher’s distribution, leading to hallucination and performance degradation. Another concern is exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) , where the student’s sampling distribution at inference time may deviate from the teacher distribution, with errors potentially accumulating across generation steps. However, the severity of exposure bias in autoregressive language models remains debated ( He et al., 2021 ) . An alternative paradigm, on-policy distillation ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , samples from the student’s own distribution rather than the teacher’s. This approach has been successfully incorporated to build powerful small language models from larger ones ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Qwen Team, 2025a ; Qwen Team, 2025b ) . However, on-policy distillation requires the student model to be sufficiently capable, as learning is limited to trajectories the student can already generate. When unifying multiple domain-specific LLMs into a single model, both distillation approaches have been explored. DeepSeek-AI (2025) employ off-policy distillation and observe that while it introduces marginal performance drops, these can be recovered through a subsequent mixed RL phase. Xiaomi LLM-Core Team (2026) incorporate on-policy distillation and achieve performance comparable to domain experts on most benchmarks. Our experiments reveal that proper initialization is critical for on-policy distillation: relying solely on SFT for initialization can lead to unstable training and final performance that falls behind domain specialists.

sections.heading: 2.2 Model Merging
sections.text: Model merging operates directly in parameter space to combine multiple task-specific LLMs into a unified model. A straightforward approach fuses the parameter deltas of different models ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent works address parameter interference through various techniques, such as neglecting minority signs ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Wan et al., 2024 ; Team, 2025 ) or applying dropout to parameter deltas ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Team, 2025 ) . Wang et al. (2026) introduce the concept of policy neighborhoods, where merging neighboring policies can improve performance. However, they demonstrate that this relationship is asymmetric and that merging non-neighboring policies may result in performance trade-offs, with gains in one task accompanied by degradation in another. An alternative approach determines optimal weights for averaging parameter deltas using metrics such as the Fisher Information Matrix ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) or task-specific evaluation metrics ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . However, these methods require additional computation and can be complex to implement.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminary
sections.text: We consider two types of distillation methods for combining single-task RL experts: off-policy distillation (Sec. 3.1 ) and on-policy distillation (Sec. 3.2 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Off-Policy Distillation
sections.text: Off-policy distillation transfers knowledge from expert teacher models to a student model by collecting rollouts generated by the teachers and training the student via supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Given a teacher model π T ​ ( y | x ) \pi_{T}(y|x) and a training prompt dataset 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} , we collect K K rollouts from each training prompt: 𝒟 rollout = ⋃ x ∈ 𝒟 train { ( x , y 1 ) , ( x , y 2 ) , … , ( x , y K ) ∣ y i ∼ π T ( ⋅ | x ) } . \mathcal{D}_{\text{rollout}}=\bigcup_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\{(x,y_{1}),(x,y_{2}),\ldots,(x,y_{K})\mid y_{i}\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot|x)\}. (1) The student model π θ ​ ( y | x ) \pi_{\theta}(y|x) is then trained to minimize the negative log-likelihood: ℒ SFT = 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ 𝒟 rollout ​ [ − log ⁡ π θ ​ ( y | x ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{rollout}}}[-\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)]. (2) This objective is equivalent to minimizing the forward KL divergence KL [ π T ∥ π θ ] \operatorname{KL}[\pi_{T}\|\pi_{\theta}] between the teacher and student distributions. In the multi-task setting, we simultaneously distill from multiple expert models, each trained specifically for a different task. Let { π T ( i ) } i = 1 N \{\pi_{T}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote the set of N N task-specific expert models. For each expert, we collect rollouts from its corresponding task dataset and merge these rollout data to form a unified training set 𝒟 multitask = ⋃ i = 1 N 𝒟 rollout ( i ) \mathcal{D}_{\text{multitask}}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{\text{rollout}}^{(i)} , where 𝒟 rollout ( i ) \mathcal{D}_{\text{rollout}}^{(i)} contains the rollouts collected from expert π T ( i ) \pi_{T}^{(i)} . The student model is then trained on this merged dataset using the SFT objective.

This requires sampling from the student model, which cannot be performed in advance. In this paper, we follow the methodology of Lu and Lab (2025) ; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team (2026) . Notably, since on-policy distillation leverages samples from the student model, it is expected that the student model already possesses adequate performance ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . In the multi-task setting, we extend on-policy distillation to simultaneously imitate multiple teacher models on their respective tasks. Specifically, each training batch contains prompts sampled from different task datasets. For a prompt from task i i , we apply the on-policy distillation objective using the corresponding teacher model π T ( i ) \pi_{T}^{(i)} to compute the reward. This allows the student model to learn from all expert models during training.

sections.heading: 4 Main Results
sections.text: We begin by presenting results for existing distillation approaches: off-policy distillation and on-policy distillation applied in isolation. On-policy distillation is initialized from SFT. We also evaluate two alternative approaches (multi-task RL and parameter merging) in Appendix B.1 .

sections.heading: Tasks and Evaluation Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate our methods on four diverse tasks spanning two domains. From τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench ( Barres et al., 2025 ) , we select two conversational agent domains: airline (booking, modifying, and canceling flight reservations and handling refunds) and telecom (technical support, bill payment, line suspension, and plan options). These tasks demand multiple agent capabilities: calling domain-specific APIs following guidelines, interacting with user agents, and dual-control (guiding the user agent to correctly invoke APIs). We also incorporate two text-based games from GEM ( Liu et al., 2025 ) : sudoku and mastermind , both using the v0-hard variant. These games require logical reasoning, planning, and memory recall over evolving game states ( Guertler et al., 2025 ) . For sudoku , we extend the max number of turns to 60. We use success rate as the evaluation metric for all tasks. For the τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench tasks, we sample 16 trajectories per test prompt and compute the average success rate. For the GEM text games, we randomly generate 128 intial setups and sample 16 trajectories for each game setup. For all 4 tasks, we report pass@1 (success rate per trajectory) and passˆ4 (probability that all 4 i.i.d. trials succeed). We perform experiments using two model scales, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 , to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach across different model capacities. For the τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench tasks, we use a locally hosted Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 model as the user simulator instead of gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 to ensure more stable and reproducible results. For the telecom domain, the user model is further fine-tuned using rejection sampling to improve its tool calling ability.

sections.heading: Off-policy distillation recovers performance of single-task RL models.
sections.text: In the single-task setting, off-policy distillation successfully recovers the performance of RL experts when applied to the same base model, demonstrating that expert trajectories can effectively transfer learned behaviors. Interetingly, the SFT phase before RL leverages data collected from claude-opus-4.5 , so it is effectively performing off-policy distillation from a stronger model. However, as presented in Fig. 1 , under a modest training budget, distilling from the RL model (which is built upon the same base model) achieves even better performance than distilling from a much stronger model. Similar observations have been made in recent work ( Gu et al., 2026 ) , attributing this to teacher models containing more modes than students can capture. Figure 1: Learning curves comparing SFT and off-policy distillation (single-task setting) on airline and telecom , where off-policy distillation is essentially SFT on teacher-generated data. Despite the SFT baseline leveraging rollouts from a substantially stronger model, off-policy distillation from RL models trained on the same base model achieves superior performance under a limited training budget. We also investigate the number of samples per prompt required for successful single-task off-policy distillation. For the telecom task, we vary the number of samples per prompt and then upsample (or downsample) to maintain a fixed dataset size of 128 × 400 128\times 400 . Notably, sampling 16 rollouts per training prompt produces 63,191 samples, exceeding 128 × 400 128\times 400 . We report telecom passˆ4 performance in Fig. 2 . We find that using fewer samples per prompt (and therefore upsampling the data) harms performance, resulting in poor results (1 sample per prompt) or high variance across trials (2-8 samples per prompt). In contrast, using 16 samples per prompt (only 1 epoch) yields much lower variance. Figure 2: Off-policy distillation performance (passˆ4) on telecom with varying samples per prompt. Dataset size fixed at 128 × 400 128\times 400 . Performance degrades with fewer samples per prompt.

sections.heading: Multi-task off-policy distillation exhibits performance degradation.
sections.text: Despite its simplicity, off-policy distillation in the multi-task setting achieves performance comparable to single-task RL models on most tasks, even surpassing them on sudoku . However, we observe notable performance degradation on telecom (8B: -2.9% passˆ4, 30B: -10.6% passˆ4), suggesting that simple aggregation of expert trajectories may not always suffice for multi-task learning. Notably, the degradation is more severe for passˆ4 than pass@1, indicating that the model struggles to consistently produce the desired behavior. Since single-task off-policy distillation achieves comparable performance to RL, we rule out exposure bias as the primary cause. Instead, we hypothesize that the root cause is the mode-covering behavior of off-policy distillation. We provide more discussion of this phenomenon in Sec. 5 .

sections.heading: On-policy distillation may require proper initialization.
sections.text: When applied directly without off-policy distillation in advance, on-policy distillation fails to achieve satisfactory performance. As shown in Tab. 2 , it exhibits substantial performance drops on telecom (-9.5% passˆ4 on 8B models, -4.2% passˆ4 on 30B models), with degradation particularly severe for the 8B model. One possible explanation is that SFT models may not provide sufficiently strong initialization for on-policy distillation. This aligns with previous findings that on-policy distillation requires the model to have sufficiently strong initial performance, as the student model must generate reasonable trajectories for effective learning ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: 5 Our Method
sections.text: Given the limitations of both distillation methods, we address two key questions: Why does off-policy distillation fail in multi-task settings? How can we robustly distill multiple experts into a unified multi-task model? We attribute the failure of off-policy distillation to the mode-covering property of forward KL divergence. In Sec. 5.1 , we present a toy example illustrating why mode-covering could become problematic in multi-task settings. Building on this insight, we propose a two-phase distillation recipe and demonstrate that our method successfully recovers the performance of single-task RL baselines. Finally, in Sec. 5.3 , we further validate our hypothesis through experiments that manipulate the off-policy distillation data.

sections.heading: 5.2 Proposed Method
sections.text: Building on our analysis, we propose a two-phase distillation approach. First, we apply off-policy distillation to establish adequate multi-task performance. Second, we apply on-policy distillation for refinement, which exploits the mode-seeking property of reverse KL divergence. This encourages the model to commit to a subset of modes that fit within the model’s limited capacity, rather than attempting to average across multiple modes. Under our two-phase method, off-policy distillation enables p 2 p_{2} to concentrate probability mass on the correct tokens 0 and 1. Consequently, leveraging the mode-seeking property of on-policy distillation, the policy may converge to either C C (copy policy) or F F (flipping policy, where each token is flipped from the previous token), both of which perfectly solve the tasks. Training curves for this toy example are provided in Appendix B.2 . For on-policy distillation, we use a batch size of 16 with 16 rollouts per training prompt. We train for 10 steps when combining two tasks ( airline and telecom ) and 30 steps when combining all four tasks. As shown in Tab. 1 and Tab. 2 , the combined approach (“Off. + On.”) successfully recovers performance across all four tasks, matching or exceeding single-task RL baselines.

sections.heading: 5.3 Empirical Validation
sections.text: To validate our hypothesis, we conduct additional experiments on tasks airline and telecom .

sections.heading: Collecting rollouts from the multi-task model.
sections.text: Instead of collecting training data from single-task RL experts, we collect rollouts from the unified multi-task model trained with our two-phase approach (Off. + On.). sections.heading: Discussions.
sections.text: Our analysis reveals that the challenges of off-policy distillation stem from the interaction between limited student model capacity and the mode-covering nature of forward KL divergence. A natural question arises: is this a genuine research problem, or will it resolve naturally as models scale? We argue that this remains an important issue for several reasons. First, given computational constraints, post-training of smaller models continues to play a crucial role in LLM research and applications. Second, as models scale, the number of modes in each single-task expert also grows with improved RL performance, maintaining the capacity mismatch. Indeed, our empirical findings in Tab. 2 demonstrate that this issue persists even in 30B-A3B models.

sections.heading: 5.4 Ablation Study on Off-Policy Distillation Data
sections.text: An important design choice in multi-task off-policy distillation is how to aggregate training data from different tasks. To investigate the impact of data mixture in off-policy distillation, we conduct experiments on airline and telecom with four different configurations: 400:400 (as in our main experiments), 400:800, 400:1200, and 800:800, where M : N M:N denotes 128 × M 128\times M samples from airline and 128 × N 128\times N samples from telecom . For each configuration, we apply an on-policy distillation phase with balanced 1:1 data mixture following off-policy distillation. The results presented in Tab. 4 reveal the following key insights. First, simply increasing data volume uniformly does not alleviate performance degradation in multi-task off-policy distillation. The 800:800 mixture exhibits similar performance drops as 400:400. Second, allocating more data to telecom can partially mitigate its performance drop, though the degradation persists (400:1200 still shows -3.3% on telecom passˆ4). Moreover, this introduces potential trade-offs with other tasks. Finally, regardless of data mixture, subsequent on-policy distillation consistently addresses the performance degradation issue across all configurations. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper investigates distillation-based methods for training multi-task agentic LLMs. Through our experiments, we reveal distinct limitations of off-policy and on-policy distillation approaches. While off-policy distillation is straightforward to implement, its mode-covering behavior makes it problematic in multi-task settings. Conversely, on-policy distillation requires the student model to already possess adequate initial performance. To address these limitations, we propose a two-phase training recipe: first applying off-policy distillation to establish adequate baseline performance, then leveraging on-policy distillation for refinement. We evaluate our method on conversational agents using τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench and text-based games in GEM, with experiments confirming the effectiveness of our approach. Additionally, we evaluate two alternative strategies: multi-task RL and parameter merging in Appendix B.1 . Under equivalent training budgets, multi-task RL underperforms distillation-based methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that parameter merging methods exhibit significant performance degradation and are highly sensitive to SFT training dynamics.

sections.heading: Appendix A Training Details
sections.text: All training is performed using the AReaL ( Fu et al., 2025 ) framework. For τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench tasks, we follow the method in Gao et al. (2026) . For 8B models, which are not covered in their paper, we adopt a batch size of 16 × 16 16\times 16 (16 training prompts with 16 rollouts each) and a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} . During training, we use Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct as the user simulator for airline and a fine-tuned Qwen3-32B model as the user simulator for telecom . We use temperature 1 for the user simulator during training and 0 for evaluation. For GEM tasks, we also use a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} . For sudoku , we adopt a batch size of 16 × 16 16\times 16 . We limit the maximum context length to 16384 during training to reduce training cost. We extend the max number of turns to 60 in evaluation. For mastermind , we adopt a batch size of 256 × 1 256\times 1 . These two tasks do not undergo SFT before RL. Consequently, when conducting on-policy distillation in the multi-task setting, the model is initialized from SFT on only the τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench tasks. All tasks have a maximum context length of 32768 during inference. For each turn, the maximum number of generated tokens is 8192.

sections.heading: B.1 Alternative Approaches
sections.text: In addition to distillation, we investigate three alternative approaches for multi-task learning: (1) off-policy distillation followed by multi-task RL; (2) parameter merging; and (3) Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . For multi-task RL, we apply the same training budget as on-policy distillation (batch size of 16 with 16 rollouts per prompt). Under this setting, we observe that RL training becomes unstable, and we report results from the best checkpoint before training collapse. For parameter merging, we evaluate three methods: naive weight averaging ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , task arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) , and DARE ( Yu et al., 2024 ) . Results are presented in Tab. 5 .

sections.heading: Multi-Task RL.
sections.text: While performance on sudoku and mastermind slightly improves compared to single-task RL baselines, the performance degradation on telecom becomes more severe. This observation aligns with previous findings that optimization across different tasks is imbalanced in the multi-task RL process ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Ramesh et al., 2026 ) , which presents substantial challenges in practical multi-task settings.

sections.heading: Parameter Merging.
sections.text: When merging experts from all four tasks, performance drops dramatically except on airline . Analysis reveals that the parameter change ‖ θ RL − θ pre ‖ 2 \|\theta_{\text{RL}}-\theta_{\text{pre}}\|_{2} for the airline expert is significantly larger than for other tasks, causing airline to dominate the merged model. Notably, this large parameter change primarily originates from the SFT process before RL, demonstrating that parameter merging can be heavily influenced by substantial parameter shifts introduced during SFT. Merging only sudoku and mastermind yields substantially better performance, though significant degradation remains compared to single-task baselines. Interestingly, we observe substantially different behavior when applying parameter merging to math and coding tasks. Using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with RL training on the boba 2 dataset ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , evaluated on AIME24 and LiveCodeBench v5 ( Jain et al., 2024 ) , all three merging methods achieve performance comparable to single-task RL (Tab. 6 ), with degradation controlled below 3.0%. This suggests that parameter merging effectiveness may be task-dependent.

We investigate whether the off-policy distillation phase is necessary, or if single-phase GKD suffices for multi-task distillation. As presented in Tab. 5 , single-phase GKD results in significant performance drop on telecom . This suggests that an off-policy distillation phase is indeed required to stabilize on-policy distillation training. In this paper, we study how to build such models by first training separate RL experts for individual tasks and then consolidating them via distillation, as an alternative to directly training a single model on mixed tasks. We show that off-policy distillation degrades in multi-task settings due to the mode-covering nature of forward KL: aggregating data from multiple tasks introduces a large number of behavioral modes that can exceed the student’s capacity, forcing it to average across behaviors and leading to degraded performance. In contrast, on-policy distillation is mode-seeking but requires strong initialization. Inspired by these observations, we propose a two-phase approach: off-policy distillation followed by on-policy refinement. Evaluation across conversational agents and text-based games confirms that this two-phase approach matches single-task RL expert performance for each individual task, whereas off-policy or on-policy distillation alone fails to match this performance. 1 Introduction Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success across a wide range of agentic large language model (LLM) tasks, including interactive tool-using agents ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , search agents ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , and text-based games ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . As an important step towards artificial general intelligence, LLMs are expected to solve multiple tasks simultaneously. However, building such unified multi-task models remains challenging. A straightforward approach is multi-task RL, i.e., jointly training a single model on multiple tasks. Unfortunately, multi-task RL presents significant practical challenges. Wu et al. (2025) find that different tasks may exhibit vastly different gradient scales, yet larger gradients do not necessarily correlate with greater performance gains. Ramesh et al. (2026) observe that certain tasks can dominate the training process, leading to suboptimal multi-task performance. Furthermore, multi-task RL may incur substantial computational costs, as the training cost of each trial is comparable to the sum of training all individual tasks. An alternative solution is to train one expert model for each task and then combine these models into a unified model. Two primary approaches exist for such combination: parameter merging ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ) and distillation ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . While parameter merging offers computational efficiency by requiring little or no additional training, it operates as a black box with limited interpretability. Parameter merging often suffers from performance trade-offs between tasks ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Empirically, we observe substantial performance degradation with parameter merging on the benchmarks we evaluate. Additionally, the effectiveness of parameter merging is highly sensitive to the training dynamics of the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase. (See Appendix B.1 for details.) This paper focuses on distillation-based methods, which provide a more interpretable paradigm for combining knowledge from different expert models. We consider two main distillation approaches: off-policy and on-policy distillation. Off-policy distillation collects rollouts from teacher models and applies supervised fine-tuning, essentially optimizing the forward KL divergence. In contrast, on-policy distillation samples from the student model and optimizes the reverse KL divergence. Limitations of Off-Policy and On-Policy Distillation. Comparing off-policy and on-policy distillation, off-policy distillation is easier to implement and offers better training stability, but prior work has identified several limitations of off-policy distillation: (1) exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , where the student model makes out-of-distribution errors during generation but receives no guidance on recovery from the training data, causing errors to accumulate across generation steps; (2) mode-covering behavior ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , which typically occurs when the teacher has larger capacity than the student—since off-policy distillation optimizes forward KL (a mode-covering objective), the student model is incentivized to place probability mass across all modes in the teacher distribution, including placing excessive probability on low-probability regions; (3) conflicting reasoning structures between teacher and student ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Among these possible limitations of off-policy distillation, our experiments reveal that when building multi-task agentic LLMs, the major challenge likely stems from its mode-covering property. Even when the student and teacher models share the same base model, aggregating data from multiple tasks introduces a larger number of behavioral modes that can exceed the student model’s capacity, forcing it to compromise by averaging across modes. Conversely, on-policy distillation cannot be applied directly without proper initialization, as it requires the student model to already possess sufficiently strong performance to generate reasonable trajectories. Our Method: Two-Phase Distillation. To address this limitation, we propose a two-phase distillation approach: off-policy distillation followed by on-policy refinement. The mode-seeking property of on-policy distillation enables the student model to focus on a subset of modes, mitigating the averaging behavior induced by off-policy distillation. Meanwhile, off-policy distillation provides the necessary initialization for on-policy distillation to generate reasonable trajectories. We evaluate our method on four tasks: two conversational agent domains from τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench ( Barres et al., 2025 ) and two text-based games from GEM ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , demonstrating that our approach successfully recovers the performance of single-task RL models. Additionally, we investigate data aggregation strategies for multi-task off-policy distillation, showing that while data mixture affects off-policy distillation performance, our two-phase approach remains robust across different mixture configurations. 2 Related Works 2.1 Knowledge Distillation Distillation transfers knowledge from a teacher model to a student model through two primary approaches. Off-policy distillation, also known as supervised knowledge distillation, collects data from the teacher model and applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . Recent successes ( Guha et al., 2025 ; Moshkov et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2025 ) have demonstrated that off-policy distillation enables small models (e.g., 1.5B parameters) to acquire strong reasoning capabilities for complex tasks in mathematics, coding, and science. However, as argued by Agarwal et al. (2024) , the mode-covering nature of forward KL divergence in off-policy distillation can cause the student to assign excessive probability mass to low-probability regions of the teacher’s distribution, leading to hallucination and performance degradation. Another concern is exposure bias ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) , where the student’s sampling distribution at inference time may deviate from the teacher distribution, with errors potentially accumulating across generation steps. However, the severity of exposure bias in autoregressive language models remains debated ( He et al., 2021 ) . An alternative paradigm, on-policy distillation ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , samples from the student’s own distribution rather than the teacher’s. This approach has been successfully incorporated to build powerful small language models from larger ones ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Qwen Team, 2025a ; Qwen Team, 2025b ) . However, on-policy distillation requires the student model to be sufficiently capable, as learning is limited to trajectories the student can already generate. When unifying multiple domain-specific LLMs into a single model, both distillation approaches have been explored. DeepSeek-AI (2025) employ off-policy distillation and observe that while it introduces marginal performance drops, these can be recovered through a subsequent mixed RL phase. Xiaomi LLM-Core Team (2026) incorporate on-policy distillation and achieve performance comparable to domain experts on most benchmarks. Our experiments reveal that proper initialization is critical for on-policy distillation: relying solely on SFT for initialization can lead to unstable training and final performance that falls behind domain specialists. 2.2 Model Merging Model merging operates directly in parameter space to combine multiple task-specific LLMs into a unified model. A straightforward approach fuses the parameter deltas of different models ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent works address parameter interference through various techniques, such as neglecting minority signs ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Wan et al., 2024 ; Team, 2025 ) or applying dropout to parameter deltas ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Team, 2025 ) . Wang et al. (2026) introduce the concept of policy neighborhoods, where merging neighboring policies can improve performance. However, they demonstrate that this relationship is asymmetric and that merging non-neighboring policies may result in performance trade-offs, with gains in one task accompanied by degradation in another. An alternative approach determines optimal weights for averaging parameter deltas using metrics such as the Fisher Information Matrix ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) or task-specific evaluation metrics ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . However, these methods require additional computation and can be complex to implement. 3 Preliminary We consider two types of distillation methods for combining single-task RL experts: off-policy distillation (Sec. 3.1 ) and on-policy distillation (Sec. 3.2 ). 3.1 Off-Policy Distillation Off-policy distillation transfers knowledge from expert teacher models to a student model by collecting rollouts generated by the teachers and training the student via supervised fine-tuning (SFT). First, we apply off-policy distillation to establish adequate multi-task performance. Second, we apply on-policy distillation for refinement, which exploits the mode-seeking property of reverse KL divergence. This encourages the model to commit to a subset of modes that fit within the model’s limited capacity, rather than attempting to average across multiple modes. Under our two-phase method, off-policy distillation enables p 2 p_{2} to concentrate probability mass on the correct tokens 0 and 1. Consequently, leveraging the mode-seeking property of on-policy distillation, the policy may converge to either C C (copy policy) or F F (flipping policy, where each token is flipped from the previous token), both of which perfectly solve the tasks. Training curves for this toy example are provided in Appendix B.2 . For on-policy distillation, we use a batch size of 16 with 16 rollouts per training prompt. We train for 10 steps when combining two tasks ( airline and telecom ) and 30 steps when combining all four tasks. Our analysis reveals that the challenges of off-policy distillation stem from the interaction between limited student model capacity and the mode-covering nature of forward KL divergence. A natural question arises: is this a genuine research problem, or will it resolve naturally as models scale? We argue that this remains an important issue for several reasons. First, given computational constraints, post-training of smaller models continues to play a crucial role in LLM research and applications. Second, as models scale, the number of modes in each single-task expert also grows with improved RL performance, maintaining the capacity mismatch. Indeed, our empirical findings in Tab. 2 demonstrate that this issue persists even in 30B-A3B models. 5.4 Ablation Study on Off-Policy Distillation Data An important design choice in multi-task off-policy distillation is how to aggregate training data from different tasks. Colored subscripts indicate performance deltas relative to single-task RL baselines. 6 Conclusion This paper investigates distillation-based methods for training multi-task agentic LLMs. Through our experiments, we reveal distinct limitations of off-policy and on-policy distillation approaches. While off-policy distillation is straightforward to implement, its mode-covering behavior makes it problematic in multi-task settings. Conversely, on-policy distillation requires the student model to already possess adequate initial performance. To address these limitations, we propose a two-phase training recipe: first applying off-policy distillation to establish adequate baseline performance, then leveraging on-policy distillation for refinement. We evaluate our method on conversational agents using τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench and text-based games in GEM, with experiments confirming the effectiveness of our approach. Additionally, we evaluate two alternative strategies: multi-task RL and parameter merging in Appendix B.1 . Under equivalent training budgets, multi-task RL underperforms distillation-based methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that parameter merging methods exhibit significant performance degradation and are highly sensitive to SFT training dynamics. References Agarwal et al. (2024) R. Appendix A Training Details All training is performed using the AReaL ( Fu et al., 2025 ) framework. For τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench tasks, we follow the method in Gao et al. (2026) . For 8B models, which are not covered in their paper, we adopt a batch size of 16 × 16 16\times 16 (16 training prompts with 16 rollouts each) and a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} . During training, we use Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct as the user simulator for airline and a fine-tuned Qwen3-32B model as the user simulator for telecom . We use temperature 1 for the user simulator during training and 0 for evaluation. For GEM tasks, we also use a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} . For sudoku , we adopt a batch size of 16 × 16 16\times 16 . We limit the maximum context length to 16384 during training to reduce training cost. We extend the max number of turns to 60 in evaluation. For mastermind , we adopt a batch size of 256 × 1 256\times 1 . These two tasks do not undergo SFT before RL. Consequently, when conducting on-policy distillation in the multi-task setting, the model is initialized from SFT on only the τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench tasks. All tasks have a maximum context length of 32768 during inference. For each turn, the maximum number of generated tokens is 8192. Appendix B Additional Results B.1 Alternative Approaches In addition to distillation, we investigate three alternative approaches for multi-task learning: (1) off-policy distillation followed by multi-task RL; (2) parameter merging; and (3) Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . For multi-task RL, we apply the same training budget as on-policy distillation (batch size of 16 with 16 rollouts per prompt). Under this setting, we observe that RL training becomes unstable, and we report results from the best checkpoint before training collapse. For parameter merging, we evaluate three methods: naive weight averaging ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , task arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) , and DARE ( Yu et al., 2024 ) . Results are presented in Tab. 5 . Multi-Task RL. While performance on sudoku and mastermind slightly improves compared to single-task RL baselines, the performance degradation on telecom becomes more severe. This observation aligns with previous findings that optimization across different tasks is imbalanced in the multi-task RL process ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Ramesh et al., 2026 ) , which presents substantial challenges in practical multi-task settings. Parameter Merging. When merging experts from all four tasks, performance drops dramatically except on airline . Analysis reveals that the parameter change ‖ θ RL − θ pre ‖ 2 \|\theta_{\text{RL}}-\theta_{\text{pre}}\|_{2} for the airline expert is significantly larger than for other tasks, causing airline to dominate the merged model. Notably, this large parameter change primarily originates from the SFT process before RL, demonstrating that parameter merging can be heavily influenced by substantial parameter shifts introduced during SFT. Merging only sudoku and mastermind yields substantially better performance, though significant degradation remains compared to single-task baselines. Interestingly, we observe substantially different behavior when applying parameter merging to math and coding tasks. Using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with RL training on the boba 2 dataset ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , evaluated on AIME24 and LiveCodeBench v5 ( Jain et al., 2024 ) , all three merging methods achieve performance comparable to single-task RL (Tab. 6 ), with degradation controlled below 3.0%. This suggests that parameter merging effectiveness may be task-dependent. Generalized Knowledge Distillation. GKD optimizes the divergence between student and teacher using samples from both the student model and the teacher model. We investigate whether the off-policy distillation phase is necessary, or if single-phase GKD suffices for multi-task distillation. As presented in Tab. 5 , single-phase GKD results in significant performance drop on telecom . This suggests that an off-policy distillation phase is indeed required to stabilize on-policy distillation training.
